paras: The manhunt for Phelp Bunyan was an armed pursuit of a young Black man in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, in August 1905, after he was accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. The Montgomery Advertiser headlined the story "LYNCHING IS FEARED," but four days later a man of nearly the same name was reported arrested and jailed at Tuscaloosa, where he denied the charge.

According to a Tuscaloosa special dated August 20, Miss Annie Barger, who lived with her aged parents about twenty miles north of the city, had gone to a spring for water on August 19 when Bunyan, described as about 18 years old, seized her. The dispatch said her screams and struggle frightened him off and that he escaped through heavy undergrowth. Armed men set out after him, and the special added that "if caught he will doubtless be summarily dealt with."
He was reported in Brookwood late on August 19 and was thought to be heading toward Tuscaloosa. The sheriff was notified and joined the search.

A second Tuscaloosa special, dated August 24, reported that "Phelp Binion" had been arrested at Holt the day before, brought to the city and placed in jail. This report said he had gone from Brookwood to Holt and signed for work there under an assumed name, and that he claimed he was "not guilty of the charge." No report of a lynching, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Coverage came from white papers only, and no Black-press account was found. The Montgomery Advertiser ran the first special under the headlines "LYNCHING IS FEARED" and "ARMED POSSEK IN PURSUIT OF BLACK BRUTE," called Bunyan "the wretch," and stated the accusation as fact. The Birmingham Age-Herald printed the same dispatch under "ARMED POSSE AFTER TUSCALOOSA NEGRO" and later headed the arrest "Negro Assailant Arrested" while still reporting his denial.

Outside Alabama, the Keowee Courier of Pickens Court House, South Carolina, carried a condensed version on August 23 under "Negro Attacks White Girl," spelling the name "Philip Binin" and predicting he would "probably be severely dealt with." Neither Alabama paper reported any action taken by the armed men after the first day.

The two Tuscaloosa reports disagree about whom the accused attacked. The first named Miss Annie Barger, attacked at a spring, while the arrest report named Mrs. Joseph Cunningham, attacked at her home while washing by a young man who had worked around her place, and did not mention Barger. The accused's name, his flight through Brookwood and the timing "last week" match in both reports, so the second may describe the same case under a different complainant or a separate charge.

reader.title: Manhunt for Phelp Bunyan
bases: Armed men pursued an accused young Black man amid stated fears of lynching, but no violence against him was reported and he was later arrested and jailed by authorities (A1, A2, A4).

The pursuit rests on one Tuscaloosa special printed in two Alabama papers and rewritten in a third (A1, A2, A3); a later special reports the arrest of a similarly named man but names a different complainant (A4).

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser called Bunyan a 'black brute' and 'the wretch', presented the accusation as fact, and wrote that he would 'doubtless be dealt with' if caught.
The Birmingham Age-Herald printed the same special with 'summarily dealt with' and later headed the arrest 'Negro Assailant Arrested' while noting his denial.
The Keowee Courier ran a condensed version headed 'Negro Attacks White Girl'.
